prompt: Let $n\ge3$ be a positive integer. Find the maximum number of diagonals of a regular $n$-gon one can select, so that any two of them do not intersect in the interior or they are perpendicular to each other.
answer: $n-2$ if $n$ is even and $n-3$ if $n$ is odd (for odd $n$ no two diagonals are perpendicular; for even $n$ induct over cyclic polygons, and use all diagonals from one vertex $A$ plus the diagonal joining the two neighbours of the vertex opposite $A$).

solutions.title: Perpendicularity criterion and induction over cyclic polygons
solutions.body:
Place the vertices at angles $\frac{2\pi j}{n}$ ($j=0,\dots,n-1$) on the circumcircle $\Gamma$. Throughout, "crossing" means meeting at an interior point of both diagonals.

**Fact 1 (non-crossing diagonals).** A family of pairwise non-crossing diagonals of a convex $m$-gon has at most $m-3$ members. *Proof by induction on $m$:* this is clear for $m=3$. If the family contains a diagonal $e$, then $e$ cuts the polygon into an $m_1$-gon and an $m_2$-gon with $m_1+m_2=m+2$, and every other member is a diagonal of one of the two parts. So the family has at most $(m_1-3)+(m_2-3)+1=m-3$ members.

**Fact 2 (when chords are perpendicular).** The chord joining the vertices with angles $\varphi,\psi$ is perpendicular to the direction $\frac{\varphi+\psi}2$. So the chords $\{i,j\}$ and $\{k,l\}$ are perpendicular if and only if $\frac{\pi(i+j-k-l)}{n}\equiv\frac\pi2\pmod\pi$, i.e. $2(i+j-k-l)$ is an odd multiple of $n$. This is impossible for odd $n$.

**Fact 3.** If two crossing chords of a circle are perpendicular, their four endpoints are not contained in a closed semicircle. Indeed, if the endpoints in circular order are $A,C,B,D$ with $AB\perp CD$, the angle between the chords is half the sum of the opposite arcs, so $\overset{\frown}{AC}+\overset{\frown}{BD}=\overset{\frown}{CB}+\overset{\frown}{DA}=180^\circ$. Hence every one of the four arcs is less than $180^\circ$, while four points in a closed semicircle leave a gap of at least $180^\circ$.

**Odd $n$.** By Fact 2, the selected diagonals must be pairwise non-crossing, so by Fact 1 there are at most $n-3$ of them. The $n-3$ diagonals from one vertex achieve this.

**Even $n$: the bound $n-2$.** We prove the more general statement: *for any convex polygon with $m\ge3$ vertices inscribed in a circle, a family $\mathcal F$ of diagonals in which any two either do not cross or are perpendicular has at most $m-2$ members.* We use induction on $m$; for $m=3$ there are no diagonals.

*(i) Some member $e$ of $\mathcal F$ crosses no other member.* Then $e$ splits the polygon into an $m_1$-gon and an $m_2$-gon ($m_1+m_2=m+2$), and every other member is a diagonal of one part. The chord $e$ cuts off an arc of at most $180^\circ$, so one part, say the $m_1$-gon, has all its vertices on a closed semicircle. By Fact 3 no two of its diagonals can cross perpendicularly, so they do not cross at all, and Fact 1 allows at most $m_1-3$ of them. The induction hypothesis allows at most $m_2-2$ in the other part. In total $|\mathcal F|\le(m_1-3)+(m_2-2)+1=m-2$.

*(ii) Every member crosses another member.* (If $\mathcal F=\varnothing$ there is nothing to prove.) Pick two crossing members $d_1\perp d_2$. Their endpoints cut $\Gamma$ into four arcs, each less than $180^\circ$ (each is complementary to the opposite arc in a sum of $180^\circ$).

First, every member is parallel to $d_1$ or to $d_2$. Suppose $e\in\mathcal F$ is parallel to neither. Then $e$ is not perpendicular to $d_1$ or $d_2$, so it crosses neither, and both endpoints of $e$ lie on one of the four closed arcs. Let $f\in\mathcal F$ cross $e$. Then $f\perp e$, so $f$ is not parallel to $d_1$ or $d_2$ either, and by the same reasoning $f$ lies on one closed arc. Because $f$ separates the endpoints of $e$, it has an endpoint strictly inside the arc between the endpoints of $e$, so $e$ and $f$ lie on the same arc. That arc is shorter than a semicircle, which contradicts Fact 3.

Now let $L_1$ be the longest member parallel to $d_1$ and $L_2$ the longest member parallel to $d_2$. *No other member has an endpoint at an endpoint $P$ of $L_1$.* Such a member $g$ would have to be perpendicular to $L_1$ (two parallel chords through $P$ coincide). Choose coordinates with $L_1$ on the line $y=h$, so $g$ lies on a vertical line through $P$ and runs from height $h$ to height $-h$. The member $g$ crosses some member $g'$, and $g'\perp g$, so $g'$ is horizontal. It crosses $g$ at an interior point, so it lies at a height $|y|<|h|$, which makes it longer than $L_1$. That is a contradiction. The same holds for $L_2$.

So the four endpoints of $L_1,L_2$ are distinct and each belongs to exactly one member. Every other vertex belongs to at most two members, one in each direction. Counting endpoints,
$$2|\mathcal F|\le4+2(m-4)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad|\mathcal F|\le m-2.$$
This completes the induction.

**Even $n$: a construction with $n-2$.** Let $A'$ be the vertex opposite $A$, and let $d'$ join the two neighbours of $A'$. Take the $n-3$ diagonals from $A$ together with $d'$. By symmetry in the line $AA'$, $d'\perp AA'$. A diagonal $AV$ crosses $d'$ only if $V$ lies strictly between the two endpoints of $d'$, i.e. $V=A'$. So the only crossing pair is $AA'$ and $d'$, and these are perpendicular. This gives $n-2$ diagonals.

**Answer: $n-2$ for even $n$, and $n-3$ for odd $n$.** ∎

prompt:
There are $n\ge3$ islands in a city. Initially, the ferry company offers some routes between some pairs of islands so that it is impossible to divide the islands into two groups such that no two islands in different groups are connected by a ferry route.

After each year, the ferry company will close a ferry route between some two islands $X$ and $Y$. At the same time, in order to maintain its service, the company will open new routes according to the following rule: for any island which is connected by a ferry route to exactly one of $X$ and $Y$, a new route between this island and the other of $X$ and $Y$ is added.

Suppose at any moment, if we partition all islands into two nonempty groups in any way, then it is known that the ferry company will close a certain route connecting two islands from the two groups after some years. Prove that after some years there will be an island which is connected to all other islands by ferry routes.
answer: Maintain two disjoint sets $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ that form a "network" (every island of $\mathcal A$ is joined to every island of $\mathcal B$). A closed $\mathcal A$–$\mathcal B$ route $AB$ gives the new network $\{A,B\}$ versus the rest, and a closed route from the network to an outside island $D$ lets $D$ join. Once the network covers all islands, the next two closures produce an island joined to everyone.

solutions.title: Grow a complete bipartite 'network'
solutions.body:
Think of islands as vertices and routes as edges. Closing $XY$ deletes the edge $XY$, and every vertex adjacent to exactly one of $X,Y$ becomes adjacent to both. Note that this operation removes only the single edge $XY$.

Call two disjoint nonempty sets $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ of islands a **network** if every island of $\mathcal A$ is joined to every island of $\mathcal B$. Edges are only ever removed one at a time, so a network stays a network until some route between $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ is closed.

**Repairing a network.** Let $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ be a network with $|\mathcal A\cup\mathcal B|\ge3$, and suppose the route $AB$ ($A\in\mathcal A$, $B\in\mathcal B$) is closed. Take $C\in\mathcal A\setminus\{A\}$. Before the closure $C$ was joined to $B$. If $C$ was also joined to $A$, both edges survive. If not, $C$ was joined to exactly one of $A,B$, so the edge $CA$ is added. Either way $C$ is joined to both $A$ and $B$ afterwards. The same holds for every $C\in\mathcal B\setminus\{B\}$. Hence
$$\mathcal A'=\{A,B\},\qquad \mathcal B'=(\mathcal A\cup\mathcal B)\setminus\{A,B\}$$
form a network ($\mathcal B'\ne\varnothing$ since $|\mathcal A\cup\mathcal B|\ge3$), with the same union. So, repairing whenever necessary, we can keep a network on a fixed set $U=\mathcal A\cup\mathcal B$ forever.

**Start.** The initial graph is connected, so there is a route $AB$. Since $n\ge3$ and the graph is connected, some third island $C$ is joined to $A$ or $B$, say to $A$. Then $\{A\},\{B,C\}$ is a network on $U=\{A,B,C\}$.

**Growing $U$.** Suppose $U\ne$ all islands. Apply the hypothesis to the partition $(U,\text{rest})$: after some years a route $AD$ with $A\in U$, $D\notin U$ is closed. Until then we keep a network $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ on $U$. Say $A\in\mathcal A$. This closure does not touch any network edge. Every $Y\in\mathcal B$ is joined to $A$, so afterwards $Y$ is joined to $D$ as well (the edge $YD$ was either there already or is added). Thus $\mathcal A\cup\{D\},\ \mathcal B$ is a network on $U\cup\{D\}$. Repeating, we eventually obtain a network on the set of all islands.

**Finish.** Now let $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ be a network containing all islands. By the hypothesis applied to $(\mathcal A,\mathcal B)$, some route $AB$ between them is eventually closed. Repairing gives the network $\{A,B\}$ versus all other islands: every other island is joined to both $A$ and $B$. Applying the hypothesis to the partition $(\{A,B\},\text{rest})$, consider the first later moment when a route between $\{A,B\}$ and the rest is closed, say $AC$ (the case $BC$ is symmetric). Up to that moment the network persists. When $AC$ is closed, $B$ keeps all its edges to the islands other than $A$, including $C$. And $B$ becomes joined to $A$: either it already was, or $B$ was joined to exactly one of $A$ and $C$ (namely $C$), so the route $BA$ is added. So $B$ is joined to every other island. ∎

prompt:
Let $n\ge2$ be an integer. In the plane, there are $n$ segments given in such a way that any two segments have an intersection point in the interior, and no three segments intersect at a single point. Jeff places a snail at one of the endpoints of each of the segments and claps his hands $n-1$ times. Each time when he claps his hands, all the snails move along their own segments and stay at the next intersection points until the next clap. Since there are $n-1$ intersection points on each segment, all snails will reach the furthest intersection points from their starting points after $n-1$ claps.

(a) Prove that if $n$ is odd then Jeff can always place the snails so that no two of them ever occupy the same intersection point.

(b) Prove that if $n$ is even then there must be a moment when some two snails occupy the same intersection point no matter how Jeff places the snails.
answer: Extend the segments to chords of a large circle; their $2n$ endpoints alternate. (a) Mark the endpoints alternately "in"/"out" around the circle and start every snail at its "in" end; a parity count shows no two meet. (b) Two neighbouring chord ends both carry snails, and those two snails meet.

prompt: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Determine the smallest positive integer $k$ with the following property: it is possible to mark $k$ cells on a $2n\times2n$ board so that there exists a unique partition of the board into $1\times2$ and $2\times1$ dominoes, none of which contains two marked cells.
answer: 2n

solutions.title: Concentric-ring construction; alternating cycles through the diagonal
solutions.body:
Number rows and columns $1,\dots,2n$; cell $(i,j)$ is in row $i$, column $j$. A domino is *allowed* if it does not contain two marked cells.

## A marking with $2n$ cells

Mark $(t,t)$ and $(t,t+1)$ for $t=1,\dots,n$. The forbidden dominoes are then exactly those formed by two consecutive cells of the staircase $(1,1),(1,2),(2,2),(2,3),\dots,(n,n),(n,n+1)$.

**The tiling $T$.** For $t=1,\dots,n$, the *ring* $R_t$ is the boundary of the square of rows and columns $t,\dots,2n+1-t$; its side has $2m=2(n-t+1)$ cells. Tile each ring as follows. Its left side (column $t$) and its right side (column $2n+1-t$), corners included, get vertical dominoes with top cells in rows $t,t+2,\dots,2n-t$. The remaining $2m-2$ cells of the top row (row $t$) and of the bottom row (row $2n+1-t$) get horizontal dominoes with left cells in columns $t+1,t+3,\dots,2n-t-1$. No domino of $T$ contains two marked cells: the marked cells of row $t$ are $(t,t)$, the top of a vertical domino whose lower cell $(t+1,t)$ is unmarked, and $(t,t+1)$, which lies in a horizontal domino with the unmarked cell $(t,t+2)$ (for $t<n$) or, for $t=n$, in the vertical domino with $(n+1,n+1)$.

**Uniqueness.** Let $P$ be any tiling by allowed dominoes. We show that every domino of $T$ belongs to $P$, taking the dominoes of $T$ in a suitable order. For each domino we exhibit a cell of it, call it the *key cell*, all of whose neighbours except its partner in $T$ are either off the board, already covered by earlier dominoes of $T$ (hence by other dominoes of $P$), or form a forbidden domino with it. Then $P$ must pair the key cell with its partner. Below, "earlier" refers to the following order:

1. Left verticals with top cell in row $i$ get time $i$, and top horizontals with left cell in column $j$ get time $j-\frac12$. Process these by increasing time.
2. Then all right verticals, by increasing row of the top cell.
3. Then all bottom horizontals, by increasing column of the left cell.

*Left vertical of $R_t$ with top cell $(i,t)$ (the key cell), time $i$.* Up: if $i>t$, the cell $(i-1,t)$ is the bottom of the previous vertical in column $t$. If $i=t$, the cell $(t-1,t)$ is the left cell of a top horizontal of $R_{t-1}$, with time $t-\frac12$, or it is off the board. Left: $(i,t-1)$ is the lower cell of the left vertical of $R_{t-1}$ with top in row $i-1$ (or it is off the board). Right: if $i=t$, then $(t,t+1)$ is marked like $(t,t)$, so that domino is forbidden. If $i>t$, then $(i,t+1)$ is the lower cell of the left vertical of $R_{t+1}$ with top in row $i-1$. All of these are earlier.

*Top horizontal of $R_t$ with left cell $(t,j)$ (the key cell), time $j-\frac12$.* Left: $(t,j-1)$ is either the corner $(t,t)$, with time $t=j-1$, or the right cell of the previous top horizontal. Up: $(t-1,j)$ is the right cell of the top horizontal of $R_{t-1}$ with left cell $(t-1,j-1)$, or it is off the board. Down: if $j=t+1$, then $(t+1,t+1)$ and $(t,t+1)$ are both marked, so that domino is forbidden. Otherwise $(t+1,j)$ is the right cell of the top horizontal of $R_{t+1}$ with left cell $(t+1,j-1)$. All of these are earlier.

*Right vertical of $R_t$ with top cell $(i,c)$, $c=2n+1-t$ (the key cell).* Up: either the previous vertical in column $c$, or, for $i=t$, the right cell $(t-1,c)$ of the last top horizontal of $R_{t-1}$ (or off the board). Right: $(i,c+1)$ is the lower cell of the right vertical of $R_{t-1}$ with top in row $i-1$ (or off the board). Left: for $i=t<n$ it is the right cell of the last top horizontal of $R_t$; for $t=n$ it is $(n,n)$, already covered; otherwise it is the lower cell of the right vertical of $R_{t+1}$ with top in row $i-1$. All of these are earlier.

*Bottom horizontal of $R_t$ with left cell $(r,j)$, $r=2n+1-t$ (the key cell).* Left: either the corner $(r,t)$, part of a left vertical, or the right cell of the previous bottom horizontal of $R_t$. Down: the right cell of the bottom horizontal of $R_{t-1}$ with left cell $(r+1,j-1)$, or off the board. Up: for $j=t+1$ the corner $(r-1,t+1)$ of $R_{t+1}$, part of a left vertical; otherwise the right cell of the bottom horizontal of $R_{t+1}$ with left cell $(r-1,j-1)$. All of these are earlier.

Hence $P=T$, and the partition is unique. So $k=2n$ is possible.

## Fewer than $2n$ marked cells never suffice

Suppose $k<2n$ cells are marked and $P$ is a valid partition. Let $\sigma$ be the reflection in the main diagonal $d$ (the cells $(i,i)$). Form a graph on the cells: join two cells by a **red** edge if they form a domino of $P$, and by a **blue** edge if their images under $\sigma$ form a domino of $P$. Blue edges also join neighbouring cells. Every cell has exactly one red and one blue edge. A red edge is never also blue, since $\sigma$ turns horizontal dominoes into vertical ones. So the graph splits into disjoint cycles of even length at least $4$, whose edges alternate in colour. The map $\sigma$ swaps red and blue edges, so it maps each cycle onto a cycle.

Let $c\in d$, and let $C$ be its cycle. Then $\sigma(C)$ contains $\sigma(c)=c$, so $\sigma(C)=C$. Also $\sigma$ swaps the two neighbours of $c$ on $C$ (the red one and the blue one), so $\sigma$ acts on $C$ as the reflection of the cycle through $c$. Such a reflection fixes exactly two vertices of the cycle: $c$ and the vertex opposite it. The cells fixed by $\sigma$ are the diagonal cells, so $C$ contains exactly two cells of $d$. Hence the $2n$ diagonal cells lie on exactly $n$ distinct cycles.

Since $k<2n$, by pigeonhole one of these $n$ cycles, $C$, contains at most one marked cell. Replace the dominoes of $P$ on $C$ (its red edges) by its blue edges. This is again a partition of the board, it differs from $P$ because $C$ has length at least $4$, and its new dominoes contain at most one marked cell each. So the partition is not unique.

**Answer: $k=2n$.** ∎

prompt:
In a convex pentagon $ABCDE$, let $F$ be a point on $AC$ such that $\angle FBC=90^\circ$. Suppose triangles $ABF$, $ACD$ and $ADE$ are similar isosceles triangles with
$$\angle FAB=\angle FBA=\angle DAC=\angle DCA=\angle EAD=\angle EDA.$$
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $CF$. Point $X$ is chosen such that $AMXE$ is a parallelogram. Show that $BD$, $EM$ and $FX$ are concurrent.
answer: $F$ lies on the circle with centre $E$ through $A$ and $D$; $B,F,E$ and $E,D,X$ are collinear; $\triangle EFA\cong\triangle MFB$ gives $\triangle EMB\cong\triangle EMX$, so $BD$ and $XF$ are mirror images in $EM$ and meet on it. (This is IMO 2016 Problem 1, stated differently there.)

solutions.title: Find the circle centred at $E$, then reflect in $EM$
solutions.body:
Let $\theta$ be the common angle. Since $F$ lies inside segment $AC$ (convexity), the rays $AF$, $AM$ and $AC$ coincide, so $\angle BAC=\angle FAD=\theta$ and $\angle CAD=\angle EAD=\theta$.

**Step 1: $EA=EF=ED$.** From $\triangle ABF\sim\triangle ACD$ we get $\frac{AB}{AF}=\frac{AC}{AD}$. Together with $\angle BAC=\angle FAD$, this gives $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle AFD$ (SAS), so
$$\angle AFD=\angle ABC=\angle ABF+\angle FBC=\theta+90^\circ.$$
In the isosceles triangle $AED$, $\angle AED=180^\circ-2\theta$, so $\angle AFD=180^\circ-\frac12\angle AED$. The diagonal $AD$ separates $E$ from $B$ and $C$, so $F$ (inside segment $AC$) lies on the other side of $AD$ from $E$. The points $Z$ on that side with $\angle AZD=180^\circ-\frac12\angle AED$ form the arc $AD$ of the circle centred at $E$ through $A$ and $D$. Hence $EF=EA=ED$.

**Step 2: $B,F,E$ are collinear and $E,D,X$ are collinear.** In the isosceles triangle $EAF$, $\angle EFA=\angle EAF=\angle EAD+\angle DAC=2\theta$. Also $\angle BFC=\angle FAB+\angle FBA=2\theta$ (exterior angle of triangle $ABF$). Since $A,F,C$ are collinear and $B,E$ lie on opposite sides of $AC$, the equality $\angle EFA=\angle BFC$ shows that the rays $FE$ and $FB$ are opposite. So $F$ lies between $B$ and $E$.

Next, $\angle EDA=\theta=\angle DAC$ with $E$ and $C$ on opposite sides of $AD$ (alternate angles), so $ED\parallel AC$, and the vector $\overrightarrow{ED}$ points in the direction of $\overrightarrow{AC}$. In the parallelogram $AMXE$ we have $\overrightarrow{EX}=\overrightarrow{AM}$, so $D$ lies on the ray $EX$.

**Step 3: two congruences.** $M$ is the midpoint of the hypotenuse $CF$ of the right triangle $FBC$, so $MF=MB$ and $\angle MBF=\angle MFB=\angle BFC=2\theta$. The triangles $EFA$ (base $FA$, base angles $2\theta$) and $MFB$ (base $FB$, base angles $2\theta$) have equal bases $FA=FB$, so they are congruent (ASA). Hence
$$EF=EA=MF=MB.$$
Now $MX=AE=MB$, using the parallelogram. Also, since $F$ lies between $B$ and $E$ and between $A$ and $M$,
$$EB=BF+FE=AF+FM=AM=EX.$$
So $E$ and $M$ are both equidistant from $B$ and $X$.

**Step 4: reflection.** The lines $EB$ and $EX$ are different, because $\angle FED=2\angle FAD=2\theta\in(0^\circ,180^\circ)$ (central and inscribed angle in the circle of Step 1). So $B\ne X$, and $EM$ is the perpendicular bisector of $BX$. The reflection in $EM$ swaps $B$ and $X$ and swaps the rays $EB$ and $EX$. Since $EF=ED$ with $F$ on ray $EB$ and $D$ on ray $EX$, it also swaps $F$ and $D$. Therefore it maps the line $BD$ onto the line $XF$.

Finally, $EM$ bisects the angle $BEX<180^\circ$, so $B$ and $D$ (on ray $EX$) lie on opposite sides of line $EM$. Hence $BD$ meets $EM$ at a point $Q$. The reflection fixes $Q$ and maps line $BD$ to line $XF$, so $Q$ lies on $XF$ too. Thus $BD$, $EM$ and $FX$ are concurrent. ∎

prompt: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with circumcircle $\Gamma$ and incentre $I$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$. Denote by $D$ the foot of perpendicular from $I$ to side $BC$. The line through $I$ perpendicular to $AI$ meets sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $F$ and $E$ respectively. Suppose the circumcircle of triangle $AEF$ intersects $\Gamma$ at a point $X$ other than $A$. Prove that lines $XD$ and $AM$ meet on $\Gamma$.
answer: Let $AM$ meet $\Gamma$ again at $Y$ and $XY$ meet $BC$ at $D'$. The chord-ratio lemma gives $\frac{BD'}{D'C}=\frac{XB}{XC}\cdot\frac{AC}{AB}$; the spiral similarity $XBF\sim XCE$ gives $\frac{XB}{XC}=\frac{BF}{CE}=\big(\frac{\sin(C/2)}{\sin(B/2)}\big)^2$; together $\frac{BD'}{D'C}=\frac{\tan(C/2)}{\tan(B/2)}=\frac{BD}{DC}$.

solutions.title: Ratio lemma and a spiral similarity
solutions.body:
Let $\beta=\frac12\angle B$ and $\gamma=\frac12\angle C$. Let $AM$ meet $\Gamma$ again at $Y$; then $Y$ lies on the arc $BC$ not containing $A$. We use directed angles $\measuredangle$ modulo $180^\circ$ where noted.

**Lemma.** If $PQRS$ is a convex cyclic quadrilateral whose diagonals meet at $T$, then $\dfrac{QT}{TS}=\dfrac{PQ\cdot QR}{PS\cdot SR}$.

*Proof.* The triangles $PQR$ and $PSR$ share the base $PR$, so $\frac{QT}{TS}=\frac{[PQR]}{[PSR]}=\frac{\frac12PQ\cdot QR\sin\angle PQR}{\frac12PS\cdot SR\sin\angle PSR}$, and $\sin\angle PQR=\sin\angle PSR$ because the two angles are supplementary. $\square$

**Step 1: $XBF$ and $XCE$ are directly similar.** Since $A,B,C,X$ are concyclic and $F\in AB$, $E\in AC$: $\measuredangle XBF=\measuredangle XBA=\measuredangle XCA=\measuredangle XCE$. Since $A,F,E,X$ are concyclic: $\measuredangle XFB=\measuredangle XFA=\measuredangle XEA=\measuredangle XEC$. So the spiral similarity $\Phi$ with centre $X$ that maps $B\mapsto C$ also maps $F\mapsto E$, and
$$\frac{XB}{XC}=\frac{BF}{CE}.\tag{1}$$

**Step 2: $X$ lies on arc $BAC$.** The rotation angle of $\Phi$ (an oriented angle mod $360^\circ$) is the angle from $\overrightarrow{BF}$ to $\overrightarrow{CE}$. These vectors point along $\overrightarrow{BA}$ and $\overrightarrow{CA}$, so the rotation angle equals the oriented angle from $\overrightarrow{AB}$ to $\overrightarrow{AC}$, which is $\pm\angle A$. It is also the oriented angle from $\overrightarrow{XB}$ to $\overrightarrow{XC}$. For $X$ on the arc $BAC$ that angle equals the oriented angle from $\overrightarrow{AB}$ to $\overrightarrow{AC}$. On the other arc it has the opposite orientation and size $180^\circ-\angle A$, which is a different oriented angle. Hence $X$ is on arc $BAC$, and $X,Y$ lie on opposite sides of $BC$. Let $XY$ meet segment $BC$ at $D'$. It suffices to prove $D'=D$.

**Step 3: the ratio $BD'/D'C$.** Apply the lemma to $ABYC$ (diagonals meet at $M$) and to $XBYC$ (diagonals meet at $D'$):
$$1=\frac{BM}{MC}=\frac{AB\cdot BY}{AC\cdot CY},\qquad \frac{BD'}{D'C}=\frac{XB\cdot BY}{XC\cdot CY}=\frac{XB}{XC}\cdot\frac{AC}{AB}.\tag{2}$$

**Step 4: compute $BF/CE$.** Since $AI\perp EF$ and $AI$ bisects $\angle A$, triangle $AFE$ is isosceles with $FI=IE$, and $\angle AFI=90^\circ-\frac A2$. In triangle $BFI$: $\angle FBI=\beta$, $\angle BFI=90^\circ+\frac A2$, so $\angle FIB=90^\circ-\beta-\frac A2=\gamma$. By the sine rule, $\frac{BF}{FI}=\frac{\sin\gamma}{\sin\beta}$. Similarly $\frac{CE}{EI}=\frac{\sin\beta}{\sin\gamma}$. Hence
$$\frac{BF}{CE}=\Big(\frac{\sin\gamma}{\sin\beta}\Big)^2.\tag{3}$$

**Step 5: conclude.** By (1), (2), (3) and $\frac{AC}{AB}=\frac{\sin2\beta}{\sin2\gamma}$,
$$\frac{BD'}{D'C}=\frac{\sin2\beta}{\sin2\gamma}\cdot\frac{\sin^2\gamma}{\sin^2\beta}=\frac{\cos\beta\,\sin\gamma}{\cos\gamma\,\sin\beta}=\frac{\tan\gamma}{\tan\beta}.$$
On the other hand, in the right triangles $BDI$ and $CDI$, $BD=\frac{ID}{\tan\beta}$ and $DC=\frac{ID}{\tan\gamma}$, so $\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{\tan\gamma}{\tan\beta}$. Both $D$ and $D'$ lie on segment $BC$ and divide it in the same ratio, so $D'=D$. Thus $X,D,Y$ are collinear, i.e. $XD$ and $AM$ meet at $Y\in\Gamma$. ∎

prompt:
Let $B=(-1,0)$ and $C=(1,0)$ be fixed points on the coordinate plane. A nonempty, bounded subset $S$ of the plane is said to be *nice* if

(i) there is a point $T$ in $S$ such that for every point $Q$ in $S$, the segment $TQ$ lies entirely in $S$; and

(ii) for any triangle $P_1P_2P_3$, there exists a unique point $A$ in $S$ and a permutation $\sigma$ of the indices $\{1,2,3\}$ for which triangles $ABC$ and $P_{\sigma(1)}P_{\sigma(2)}P_{\sigma(3)}$ are similar.

Prove that there exist two distinct nice subsets $S$ and $S'$ of the set $\{(x,y):x\ge0,\ y\ge0\}$ such that if $A\in S$ and $A'\in S'$ are the unique choices of points in (ii), then the product $BA\cdot BA'$ is a constant independent of the triangle $P_1P_2P_3$.
answer: Take $S=\{x,y\ge0,\ (x+1)^2+y^2\le4\}$ (where $BC$ is the longest side and $AB\ge AC$) and $S'=\{x,y\ge0,\ (x+1)^2+y^2\ge4,\ (x-1)^2+y^2\le4\}$ (where $BC$ is the middle side), star-shaped from $(1,2)$. If the sides are $p\ge q\ge r$, then $BA=\frac{2q}{p}$ and $BA'=\frac{2p}{q}$, so $BA\cdot BA'=4$.

solutions.title: Let $BC$ play the longest side in $S$ and the middle side in $S'$
solutions.body:
Points of the first quadrant satisfy $AB\ge AC$ (since $x\ge0$). Define
$$S=\{(x,y):x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ (x+1)^2+y^2\le4\},$$
$$S'=\{(x,y):x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ (x+1)^2+y^2\ge4,\ (x-1)^2+y^2\le4\}.$$
For $A\in S$ we have $BC=2\ge AB\ge AC$, and for $A'\in S'$ we have $A'B\ge2=BC\ge A'C$. Both sets are bounded, nonempty and different (for example $(0,0)\in S\setminus S'$).

**Condition (ii) for $S$.** Let the side lengths of $P_1P_2P_3$ be $p\ge q\ge r$. If $A\in S$ and $ABC$ is similar to the triangle, then the sorted side lengths $(BC,AB,AC)$ of $ABC$ must be proportional to $(p,q,r)$. Hence $AB=\frac{2q}p$ and $AC=\frac{2r}p$. A nondegenerate triangle needs $y>0$, and in the upper half-plane there is exactly one point with these distances to $B$ and $C$. So $A$ is unique. Conversely, that point satisfies $AB\le2$ and $AB\ge AC$, so it lies in $S$. Points of $S$ with $y=0$ give degenerate triangles and never qualify.

**Condition (ii) for $S'$.** In the same way, $A'\in S'$ forces $(A'B,BC,A'C)$ to be proportional to $(p,q,r)$, so $A'B=\frac{2p}q$ and $A'C=\frac{2r}q$. Exactly one point of the upper half-plane has these distances, and it satisfies $A'B\ge2\ge A'C$ and $A'B\ge A'C$, so it lies in $S'$.

**Condition (i).** $S$ is convex (the intersection of a disc and a quadrant), so any $T\in S$ works. For $S'$ take $T'=(1,2)$, which lies in $S'$. Let $Q=(q_1,q_2)\in S'$. The segment $T'Q$ stays in the quadrant and in the disc $(x-1)^2+y^2\le4$, since these sets are convex. It remains to show that $|Z-B|\ge2$ for every point $Z=T'+s(Q-T')$ with $0\le s\le1$. Put $u=q_1-1$ and $v=q_2-2$. Since $T'-B=(2,2)$,
$$g(s)=|Z-B|^2=(2+su)^2+(2+sv)^2=8+4s(u+v)+s^2(u^2+v^2).$$
- If $u+v\ge0$, then $g(s)\ge8$.
- If $u+v<0$ and $uv\le0$, then for all real $s$, $g(s)\ge8-\frac{4(u+v)^2}{u^2+v^2}\ge4$, because $(u+v)^2=u^2+v^2+2uv\le u^2+v^2$.
- If $u,v<0$, i.e. $0\le q_1<1$ and $0\le q_2<2$, then $(u+1)^2+(v+1)^2=q_1^2+(q_2-1)^2<2$. This is equivalent to $-2(u+v)>u^2+v^2$, so the vertex of the parabola $g$ lies at $s>1$. Then $g$ is decreasing on $[0,1]$, and $g(s)\ge g(1)=|Q-B|^2\ge4$.

So $T'Q\subset S'$, and both sets are nice.

**The product.** With $p\ge q\ge r$ as above,
$$BA\cdot BA'=\frac{2q}{p}\cdot\frac{2p}{q}=4,$$
independent of the triangle. ∎

prompt: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB=AC\ne BC$ and let $I$ be its incentre. The line $BI$ meets $AC$ at $D$, and the line through $D$ perpendicular to $AC$ meets $AI$ at $E$. Prove that the reflection of $I$ in $AC$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $BDE$.
answer: With $I'$ the reflection, $DE$ is the external bisector of $\angle BDI'$, so it suffices to show $EB=EI'$. With $T,M$ the touch points of the incircle on $AB,BC$: $DT=DM$, and the similar triangles $DAT\sim EAI'$ and $DAM\sim EAB$ give $EI'=DT\cdot\frac{AI}{AT}$ and $EB=DM\cdot\frac{AB}{AM}$, where $\frac{AI}{AT}=\frac{AB}{AM}$.

solutions.title: Reduce to $EB=EI'$ and use similar triangles
solutions.body:
Let $I'$ be the reflection of $I$ in $AC$, and let $\alpha=\frac12\angle BAC$.

**Reduction.** The ray $DI$ is the ray $DB$ (because $I$ lies between $B$ and $D$), and $DI'$ is its mirror image in $AC$. So line $AC$ bisects $\angle BDI'$, and $DE\perp AC$ is the external bisector of $\angle BDI'$. The external bisector at $D$ meets the circumcircle of $BDI'$ again at the midpoint $N$ of the arc $BDI'$, which satisfies $NB=NI'$. Since $DB=DI+IB>DI=DI'$, the external bisector is not the perpendicular bisector of $BI'$, so these two lines meet only at $N$. Hence, **if $EB=EI'$, then $E=N$ lies on the circle $BDI'$**, which is the claim. We prove $EB=EI'$.

**Notation.** Let the incircle touch $AB$ at $T$ and $BC$ at $M$. Because $AB=AC$, $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$, and $A,I,M$ are collinear with $AM\perp BC$.

**(1) $DT=DM$.** $BT=BM$ and $BI$ bisects $\angle TBM$, so $BI$ is the perpendicular bisector of $TM$. Since $D\in BI$, $DT=DM$.

**(2) $EI'=DT\cdot\frac{AI}{AT}$.** The right triangles $ADE$ (right angle at $D$) and $ATI$ (right angle at $T$) have $\angle DAE=\angle TAI=\alpha$, so $\frac{AD}{AE}=\frac{AT}{AI}=\frac{AT}{AI'}$. Also $\angle DAT=2\alpha=\angle EAC+\angle CAI'=\angle EAI'$. So $\triangle DAT\sim\triangle EAI'$ (SAS), and $\frac{DT}{EI'}=\frac{AD}{AE}=\frac{AT}{AI}$.

**(3) $EB=DM\cdot\frac{AB}{AM}$.** The right triangles $AMB$ and $ATI$ share the angle $\alpha$ at $A$, so $\frac{AM}{AB}=\frac{AT}{AI}=\frac{AD}{AE}$. Hence $\frac{AD}{AM}=\frac{AE}{AB}$, and $\angle DAM=\alpha=\angle EAB$, so $\triangle DAM\sim\triangle EAB$ and $\frac{DM}{EB}=\frac{AD}{AE}=\frac{AM}{AB}$.

**Conclusion.** From (2) and (3), $EI'=DT\cdot\frac{AI}{AT}$ and $EB=DM\cdot\frac{AB}{AM}$. Here $DT=DM$ by (1) and $\frac{AI}{AT}=\frac{AB}{AM}$ by (3). Hence $EB=EI'$, and by the reduction $I'$ lies on the circumcircle of $BDE$. ∎

prompt: Let $D$ be the foot of perpendicular from $A$ to the Euler line (the line passing through the circumcentre and the orthocentre) of an acute scalene triangle $ABC$. A circle $\omega$ with centre $S$ passes through $A$ and $D$, and it intersects sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $X$ and $Y$ respectively. Let $P$ be the foot of altitude from $A$ to $BC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Prove that the circumcentre of triangle $XSY$ is equidistant from $P$ and $M$.
answer: As $S$ moves on the perpendicular bisector of $AD$, the spiral similarity about $D$ carrying one configuration $(S,X,Y)$ to another shows that the circumcentre $O_1$ of $XSY$ is the image of $S$ under a fixed similarity, so $O_1$ moves on a line. For $S$ the midpoint of $AH$ (giving the nine-point centre) and for $S$ the midpoint of $AO$ (giving a point on the perpendicular bisector of the midline), $O_1$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $PM$; so that line is the whole locus.

solutions.title: Linearity of the locus and two special positions
solutions.body:
Let $H$ and $O$ be the orthocentre and circumcentre, so the Euler line is $OH$ (and $O\ne H$, the triangle being scalene). Every admissible centre $S$ lies on the perpendicular bisector $\ell$ of $AD$. For $S\in\ell$, let $X_S,Y_S$ be the second intersections of the circle $\omega_S$ (centre $S$, through $A$ and $D$) with lines $AB,AC$, and let $O_S$ be the circumcentre of $X_SSY_S$. Let $m$ be the perpendicular bisector of $PM$. We must show $O_S\in m$. Directed angles are taken mod $180^\circ$.

**Step 1: $O_S$ is the image of $S$ under a fixed similarity.** Fix $S_0\in\ell$ and let $S\in\ell$ be arbitrary.
- The circles $\omega_{S_0}$ and $\omega_S$ meet at $A$ and $D$, and $X_{S_0},X_S$ lie on one line through $A$, as do $Y_{S_0},Y_S$. By the standard lemma on spiral similarities, the spiral similarity $\phi$ with centre $D$ mapping $X_{S_0}\mapsto X_S$ also maps $Y_{S_0}\mapsto Y_S$.
- In the isosceles triangle $X_SSY_S$, the central angle is twice the inscribed angle at $A$, so $\measuredangle SX_SY_S=90^\circ-\measuredangle X_SAY_S=90^\circ-\measuredangle(AB,AC)$, and similarly at $Y_S$. These angles do not depend on $S$, so the triangles $S_0X_{S_0}Y_{S_0}$ and $SX_SY_S$ are directly similar. Hence $\phi$ maps $S_0\mapsto S$ and the circumcentre $O_{S_0}\mapsto O_S$.
- Since $\phi$ is a spiral similarity about $D$, the triangles $DS_0O_{S_0}$ and $DSO_S$ are directly similar. So $O_S=\psi(S)$, where $\psi$ is the fixed spiral similarity about $D$ that maps $S_0$ to $O_{S_0}$.

Consequently, as $S$ runs along the line $\ell$, the point $O_S$ runs along the line $\psi(\ell)$. Since $\psi$ is injective, distinct centres give distinct points $O_S$.

**Step 2: two special centres.** Since $\angle ADH=\angle ADO=90^\circ$, the point $D$ lies on the circles with diameters $AH$ and $AO$. So the midpoints $S_1$ of $AH$ and $S_2$ of $AO$ lie on $\ell$, and $S_1\ne S_2$.

- $S=S_1$: $\omega$ is the circle with diameter $AH$. It meets $AB$ at the point $X$ with $HX\perp AB$, which is the foot of the altitude from $C$, and similarly $Y$ is the foot of the altitude from $B$ (both on the sides, as the triangle is acute). The nine-point circle passes through $X$, $Y$ and the midpoint $S_1$ of $AH$, so $O_{S_1}$ is the nine-point centre. The nine-point circle also passes through $P$ and $M$, so $O_{S_1}\in m$.
- $S=S_2$: $\omega$ is the circle with diameter $AO$. It meets $AB,AC$ at the feet of the perpendiculars from $O$, i.e. at the midpoints $X'$ of $AB$ and $Y'$ of $AC$. Since $X'Y'\parallel BC$, the perpendicular bisector of $X'Y'$ is perpendicular to $BC$. It passes through the point of $BC$ whose position is the average of the projections of $X'=\frac{A+B}2$ and $Y'=\frac{A+C}2$ onto $BC$, namely $\frac{P+M}2$. So it is exactly $m$, and $O_{S_2}\in m$.

**Conclusion.** The line $\psi(\ell)$ contains the two distinct points $O_{S_1},O_{S_2}$ of $m$, so $\psi(\ell)=m$. Hence for every admissible $S$, the circumcentre of $XSY$ lies on $m$, i.e. it is equidistant from $P$ and $M$. ∎

prompt: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $\angle ABC=\angle ADC<90^\circ$. The internal angle bisectors of $\angle ABC$ and $\angle ADC$ meet $AC$ at $E$ and $F$ respectively, and meet each other at point $P$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AC$ and let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $BPD$. Segments $BM$ and $DM$ intersect $\omega$ again at $X$ and $Y$ respectively. Denote by $Q$ the intersection point of lines $XE$ and $YF$. Prove that $PQ\perp AC$.
answer: $Y$ lies on circle $ABC$ and $MY\cdot MD=MA^2$, so $YF$ bisects $\angle AYC$ and $YB'$ (with $B'$ the arc midpoint) is the external bisector. The line through $P$ parallel to $AC$ meets $\omega$ again at a point $S$ on $YB'$, and similarly on the external bisector at $X$. Hence $\angle QYS=\angle QXS=90^\circ$, $QS$ is a diameter of $\omega$, and $PQ\perp PS\parallel AC$.

solutions.title: Locate $Y$ on circle $ABC$, then find the antipode of $Q$
solutions.body:
Let $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ be the circumcircles of $ABC$ and $ADC$, and let $\varphi=\angle ABC=\angle ADC$. We use directed angles $\measuredangle$ modulo $180^\circ$. Since $B$ and $D$ lie on opposite sides of $AC$, the equal angles give $\measuredangle ABC=\measuredangle CDA$.

**Step 1: $Z=AD\cap BC$ lies on $\omega$.** If $AD\parallel BC$, then $\angle BAD=\angle BCD$ and $ABCD$ would be a parallelogram, whose bisectors at $B$ and $D$ are parallel; so $Z$ exists. Orient the plane so that $\measuredangle ABC=+\varphi$. The internal bisectors give $\measuredangle PDA=\measuredangle PBC=\frac\varphi2$, i.e. $\measuredangle PDZ=\measuredangle PBZ$. Hence $Z\in\omega$.

**Step 2: $Y\in\omega_1$ and $MY\cdot MD=MA^2$.** Let $Y'$ be the point of ray $MD$ with $MY'\cdot MD=MA^2=MC^2$. Then $\triangle MAY'$ and $\triangle MDA$ are oppositely similar (common angle at $M$, $\frac{MA}{MD}=\frac{MY'}{MA}$), and likewise $\triangle MCY'$ and $\triangle MDC$. Therefore
$$\measuredangle AY'C=\measuredangle AY'M+\measuredangle MY'C=\measuredangle MAD+\measuredangle DCM=\measuredangle CAD+\measuredangle DCA=\measuredangle CDA=\measuredangle ABC,$$
so $Y'\in\omega_1$. Next, $\measuredangle Y'BZ=\measuredangle Y'BC=\measuredangle Y'AC=\measuredangle Y'AM=\measuredangle MDA=\measuredangle Y'DZ$, using the opposite similarity in the fourth step. So $Y'$ lies on the circle $BDZ=\omega$. As $\angle ADC\ne90^\circ$, we have $MD\ne MA$, so $Y'\ne D$. Hence $Y'$ is the second intersection of $DM$ with $\omega$: $Y=Y'$.

In the same way (exchange the roles of $B$ and $D$) we get $X\in\omega_2$, $MX\cdot MB=MA^2$ and $\triangle MAX\sim\triangle MBA$, $\triangle MCX\sim\triangle MBC$.

**Step 3: $YF$ and $XE$ are internal bisectors.** From the similar triangles, $AY=AD\cdot\frac{MA}{MD}$ and $CY=CD\cdot\frac{MC}{MD}$. Since $MA=MC$, $\frac{YA}{YC}=\frac{AD}{CD}=\frac{FA}{FC}$ by the angle bisector theorem in $ADC$. So $YF$ is the internal bisector of $\angle AYC$. Similarly $XE$ is the internal bisector of $\angle AXC$.

**Step 4: the external bisectors.** Let $B'$ be the second intersection of line $BP$ with $\omega_1$; it is the midpoint of the arc $AC$ not containing $B$. The point $Y$ lies on ray $MD$, i.e. on the arc $AC$ not containing $B$. So $B'$ is the midpoint of the arc $AC$ containing $Y$, and $YB'$ is the external bisector of $\angle AYC$: $YB'\perp YF$. Similarly, with $D'$ the second intersection of $DP$ with $\omega_2$, $XD'\perp XE$.

**Step 5: a common point $S$.** Let $l$ be the line through $P$ parallel to $AC$, and let $S$ be its second intersection with $\omega$ ($S=P$ if $l$ is tangent). Then $\measuredangle(l,SY)=\measuredangle PSY=\measuredangle PBY$ (with the tangent–chord angle if $S=P$). On the other hand,
$$\measuredangle(AC,B'Y)=\measuredangle ACY+\measuredangle CYB'=\measuredangle ACY+\measuredangle CAB'=\measuredangle ACY+\measuredangle B'CA=\measuredangle B'CY=\measuredangle B'BY=\measuredangle PBY,$$
using $B'A=B'C$ and the circle $\omega_1$. Since $l\parallel AC$, the lines $SY$ and $B'Y$ make the same angle with $l$ and share the point $Y$, so they coincide: $S\in YB'$. In the same way, $S\in XD'$.

**Step 6: conclusion.** Now $QY\perp YS$ and $QX\perp XS$, so $X$ and $Y$ lie on the circle with diameter $QS$. This circle passes through $X,Y,S\in\omega$, so it is $\omega$, and $QS$ is a diameter of $\omega$. Since $P\in\omega$, we get $PQ\perp PS=l$ (if $S=P$, then $l$ is the tangent at the end $P$ of the diameter $PQ$, and again $PQ\perp l$). As $l\parallel AC$, we conclude $PQ\perp AC$. ∎

prompt:
Let $I$ be the incentre of a non-equilateral triangle $ABC$, $I_A$ be the $A$-excentre, $I'_A$ be the reflection of $I_A$ in $BC$, and $l_A$ be the reflection of line $AI'_A$ in $AI$. Define points $I_B$, $I'_B$ and line $l_B$ analogously. Let $P$ be the intersection point of $l_A$ and $l_B$.

(a) Prove that $P$ lies on line $OI$ where $O$ is the circumcentre of triangle $ABC$.

(b) Let one of the tangents from $P$ to the incircle of triangle $ABC$ meet the circumcircle at points $X$ and $Y$. Show that $\angle XIY=120^\circ$.
answer: (a) $P$ is the inverse $P^*$ of $I$ in the circumcircle: $P^*$ lies on ray $OI$ with $OP^*=\frac{R^2}{OI}$. Power of a point gives $A,M,O,P^*$ concyclic ($M$ the arc midpoint), and an angle chase via $\triangle AA'I_A\sim\triangle AIO$ ($A'$ the reflection of $A$ in $BC$) puts $P^*$ on $l_A$; likewise on $l_B$. (b) Euler's $OI^2=R^2-2Rr$ gives distance $R/2$ from $O$ to $XY$, so $\angle XOY=120^\circ$; and $PX\cdot PY=PI\cdot PO$ makes $X,Y,I,O$ concyclic.

solutions.title: $P$ is the inverse of $I$ in the circumcircle
solutions.body:
Let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle, with radius $R$; let $r$ be the inradius. Let $M$ be the second intersection of $AI$ with $\Gamma$ (the midpoint of arc $BC$), and $A'$ the reflection of $A$ in $BC$. Since the triangle is not equilateral, $O\ne I$. Let $P^*$ be the point on ray $OI$ with $OP^*\cdot OI=R^2$, the inverse of $I$ in $\Gamma$. Note that $P^*$ lies beyond $I$, since $OI<R$. Directed angles $\measuredangle$ are taken mod $180^\circ$.

## (a)

**Claim: $P^*\in l_A$.** If $A$ lies on line $OI$, then $AO$ and $AI$ coincide; since the altitude $AA'$ is the reflection of $AO$ in $AI$, we get $AB=AC$. Then $I_A,I'_A$ lie on $AI$, so $l_A=AI=OI\ni P^*$. Now assume $A\notin OI$.

*Two similar triangles.* We have $AA'=2h_a=\frac{bc}R$. Also $AI\cdot AI_A=bc$, because $\triangle ABI_A\sim\triangle AIC$ (angles $\frac A2$ at $A$, and $\angle ABI_A=90^\circ+\frac B2=\angle AIC$). So $AA'\cdot AO=AI\cdot AI_A$, i.e. $\frac{AA'}{AI}=\frac{AI_A}{AO}$. The altitude $AA'$ and $AO$ are symmetric about the bisector $AI$, so the rotation taking ray $AA'$ to ray $AI_A$ equals the rotation taking ray $AI$ to ray $AO$. Hence $\triangle AA'I_A$ and $\triangle AIO$ are *directly* similar (with $A'\leftrightarrow I$, $I_A\leftrightarrow O$), and $\measuredangle AA'I_A=\measuredangle AIO$.

*Angle of $l_A$.* Since $l_A$ is the mirror image of $AI'_A$ in line $AM$,
$$\measuredangle(AM,l_A)=\measuredangle(AI'_A,AM)=\measuredangle I'_AAA'-\measuredangle I_AAA'.$$
The reflection in $BC$ swaps $A\leftrightarrow A'$ and $I_A\leftrightarrow I'_A$, so $\measuredangle I'_AAA'=\measuredangle AA'I_A=\measuredangle AIO$. Also $AA'\parallel OM$ (both are perpendicular to $BC$), so $\measuredangle I_AAA'=\measuredangle(AM,OM)$. Therefore
$$\measuredangle(AM,l_A)=\measuredangle(AM,OI)-\measuredangle(AM,OM)=\measuredangle(OM,OI)=\measuredangle MOP^*.$$

*Concyclicity.* The point $I$ lies between $A$ and $M$ and between $O$ and $P^*$, and
$$IA\cdot IM=R^2-OI^2=OI\,(OP^*-OI)=IO\cdot IP^*$$
(the power of $I$ with respect to $\Gamma$). By the converse of the power of a point, $A,M,O,P^*$ are concyclic, so $\measuredangle(AM,AP^*)=\measuredangle MAP^*=\measuredangle MOP^*$. Hence the lines $AP^*$ and $l_A$ through $A$ make the same angle with $AM$, so they coincide, and $P^*\in l_A$.

In the same way $P^*\in l_B$. The lines $l_A$ and $l_B$ are distinct, because they meet at the single point $P$. So $P=P^*$, which lies on line $OI$.

## (b)

We have $PO=\frac{R^2}{OI}$ and $PI=PO-OI=\frac{R^2-OI^2}{OI}$, and Euler's formula gives $R^2-OI^2=2Rr$. Let the tangent touch the incircle at $T$, and let $D$ be the midpoint of $XY$. Then $IT\perp XY$ and $OD\perp XY$. The points $I$ and $O$ lie on one ray from $P\in XY$, so their distances to line $XY$ are proportional to $PI$ and $PO$:
$$OD=IT\cdot\frac{PO}{PI}=r\cdot\frac{R^2}{R^2-OI^2}=r\cdot\frac{R^2}{2Rr}=\frac R2.$$
So $\cos\angle XOD=\frac{OD}{OX}=\frac12$, and $\angle XOY=2\angle XOD=120^\circ$.

Moreover $PX\cdot PY=PO^2-R^2=\frac{R^2(R^2-OI^2)}{OI^2}=PO\cdot PI$. Here $X,Y$ lie on one ray from $P$ and $I,O$ on another, so $X,Y,I,O$ are concyclic. Since $I$ and $O$ lie on the same side of $XY$, the inscribed angles over $XY$ are equal: $\angle XIY=\angle XOY=120^\circ$. ∎

prompt:
Let $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$ be points on sides $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ of an acute triangle $ABC$ respectively, such that $AA_1$, $BB_1$ and $CC_1$ are the internal angle bisectors of triangle $ABC$. Let $I$ be the incentre of triangle $ABC$, and $H$ be the orthocentre of triangle $A_1B_1C_1$. Show that
$$AH+BH+CH\ge AI+BI+CI.$$
answer: With $\alpha\le\beta\le\gamma$: $A_1B_1C_1$ is acute, and comparing the segments cut off by the bisectors locates $H$ in triangle $AIC_1$. By convexity of $f(Z)=AZ+BZ+CZ$, $f(H)\ge f(I)+\nabla f(I)\cdot(H-I)$, and $\nabla f(I)$ has nonnegative dot product with $\overrightarrow{IA}$ and $\overrightarrow{IC_1}$ because $\sin\frac\beta2+\sin\frac\gamma2\ge1\ge\sin\frac\alpha2+\sin\frac\beta2$.

solutions.title: Locate $H$, then use convexity of $AZ+BZ+CZ$
solutions.body:
Let $\alpha=\angle A\le\beta=\angle B\le\gamma=\angle C$ (all less than $90^\circ$), with $a=BC$, $b=CA$, $c=AB$, so $a\le b\le c$. By the angle bisector theorem,
$$BA_1=\tfrac{ca}{b+c},\ BC_1=\tfrac{ca}{a+b},\quad CA_1=\tfrac{ab}{b+c},\ CB_1=\tfrac{ab}{a+c},\quad AB_1=\tfrac{bc}{a+c},\ AC_1=\tfrac{bc}{a+b}.$$

**Step 1: triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ is acute.** Take $D,E$ on $BC$ with $B_1D\parallel AB$ and $B_1E$ bisecting $\angle BB_1C$. In triangle $BB_1D$ the angle at $D$ equals $180^\circ-\beta>90^\circ$, so $BB_1>B_1D$. Since $\triangle CDB_1\sim\triangle CBA$, we have $\frac{DB_1}{B_1C}=\frac{BA}{AC}$. Hence
$$\frac{BE}{EC}=\frac{BB_1}{B_1C}>\frac{DB_1}{B_1C}=\frac{BA}{AC}=\frac{BA_1}{A_1C},$$
so $BA_1<BE$ and $\angle BB_1A_1<\angle BB_1E=\frac12\angle BB_1C$. In the same way $\angle BB_1C_1<\frac12\angle BB_1A$. Adding,
$$\angle A_1B_1C_1<\tfrac12(\angle BB_1C+\angle BB_1A)=90^\circ.$$
The same argument works at $A_1$ and $C_1$. So $H$ lies inside triangle $A_1B_1C_1$, on each of its altitudes between the vertex and the foot.

**Step 2: $H$ lies in triangle $AIC_1$.** At vertex $B$: $BA_1\le BC_1$ (as $a+b\le b+c$), so in triangle $BA_1C_1$ we get $\angle BC_1A_1\le\angle BA_1C_1$. Let $F=BB_1\cap A_1C_1$. Since $BF$ bisects $\angle A_1BC_1$, this gives $\angle BFA_1\le\angle BFC_1$, so $\angle B_1FC_1=\angle BFA_1\le90^\circ$. Hence the foot of the altitude from $B_1$ lies on segment $FC_1$, and $H$ (on that altitude, between $B_1$ and the foot) lies in the closed half-plane of line $BB_1$ containing $C_1$, i.e. on $A$'s side.

The same argument at $C$ (where $CA_1\le CB_1$, as $a+c\le b+c$) puts $H$ on $B_1$'s side of $CC_1$, i.e. on $A$'s side. At $A$ (where $AB_1\le AC_1$, as $a+b\le a+c$) it puts $H$ on $C_1$'s side of $AA_1$, i.e. on $B$'s side. Within triangle $ABC$, these three half-planes meet in triangle $AIC_1$. So
$$H-I=\lambda\,(A-I)+\mu\,(C_1-I)\qquad\text{for some }\lambda,\mu\ge0.$$

**Step 3: a convexity estimate.** Let $f(Z)=AZ+BZ+CZ$, and let $e_A,e_B,e_C$ be the unit vectors along $\overrightarrow{AI},\overrightarrow{BI},\overrightarrow{CI}$. For each vertex $V$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|Z-V|\ge e_V\cdot(Z-V)=|I-V|+e_V\cdot(Z-I)$. Summing,
$$f(Z)\ge f(I)+g\cdot(Z-I),\qquad g=e_A+e_B+e_C.$$
So it suffices to prove $g\cdot(A-I)\ge0$ and $g\cdot(C_1-I)\ge0$, i.e. $g\cdot(-e_A)\ge0$ and $g\cdot e_C\ge0$ (since $A-I$ is a positive multiple of $-e_A$, and $C_1-I$ a positive multiple of $e_C$).

The angle between $e_A$ and $e_B$ is $\angle AIB=90^\circ+\frac\gamma2$, so $e_A\cdot e_B=-\sin\frac\gamma2$. Similarly $e_A\cdot e_C=-\sin\frac\beta2$ and $e_B\cdot e_C=-\sin\frac\alpha2$. Thus
$$g\cdot(-e_A)=\sin\tfrac\beta2+\sin\tfrac\gamma2-1,\qquad g\cdot e_C=1-\sin\tfrac\alpha2-\sin\tfrac\beta2.$$

*$\sin\frac\alpha2+\sin\frac\beta2\le1$:* since $\gamma\ge60^\circ$, $\alpha+\beta\le120^\circ$, and
$$\sin\tfrac\alpha2+\sin\tfrac\beta2=2\sin\tfrac{\alpha+\beta}4\cos\tfrac{\alpha-\beta}4\le2\sin30^\circ=1.$$

*$\sin\frac\beta2+\sin\frac\gamma2\ge1$:* if $\beta\ge60^\circ$, both terms are at least $\frac12$. If $\beta<60^\circ$, then $\gamma=180^\circ-\alpha-\beta\ge180^\circ-2\beta$, so $\frac\gamma2\ge90^\circ-\beta$ and $\sin\frac\gamma2\ge\cos\beta=1-2s^2$, where $s=\sin\frac\beta2<\frac12$. Then $\sin\frac\beta2+\sin\frac\gamma2\ge1+s(1-2s)\ge1$.

Therefore $g\cdot(H-I)=\lambda\,g\cdot(A-I)+\mu\,g\cdot(C_1-I)\ge0$, and
$$AH+BH+CH=f(H)\ge f(I)=AI+BI+CI.$$
∎

prompt:
For any positive integer $k$, denote the sum of digits of $k$ in its decimal representation by $S(k)$. Find all polynomials $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that for any positive integer $n\ge2016$, the integer $P(n)$ is positive and
$$S(P(n))=P(S(n)).$$
answer: $P(x)=c$ with $c\in\{1,2,\dots,9\}$, and $P(x)=x$.

solutions.title: Split by degree
solutions.body:
**Constant $P=c$.** The condition says $S(c)=c$ with $c>0$, which holds exactly for $1\le c\le9$ (for $c\ge10$ we have $S(c)<c$).

**Degree at least $2$.** Let $P$ have degree $d\ge2$ and leading coefficient $a_d>0$ (positive, since $P(n)>0$ for large $n$). Take $n=10^k-1$ with $k$ large, so $S(n)=9k$. Since $P(n)<Cn^d<10^{dk+c_0}$ for constants $C,c_0$, the number $P(n)$ has at most $dk+c_0$ digits, so $S(P(n))\le9(dk+c_0)$, which is linear in $k$. But $P(S(n))=P(9k)\ge\frac{a_d}2(9k)^d$ for large $k$, which grows at least quadratically. So $S(P(n))=P(S(n))$ fails for large $k$.

**Degree $1$.** Let $P(x)=ax+b$ with $a\ge1$. Recall $S(u+v)\le S(u)+S(v)$ for positive integers $u,v$ (carries only decrease the digit sum). Using $n=2025$ and $n=2020$:
$$S(2025a+b)-S(2020a+b)=a\big(S(2025)-S(2020)\big)=5a,$$
while $S(2025a+b)=S\big((2020a+b)+5a\big)\le S(2020a+b)+S(5a)$. Hence $5a\le S(5a)$. This forces $5a\le9$, so $a=1$, and the condition becomes
$$S(n+b)=S(n)+b\qquad(n\ge2016).$$
- If $b>0$, take $n=10^k-b$ with $k$ large: $1=S(10^k)=S(n)+b\ge1+b$, which is impossible.
- If $b<0$, take $n=10^k$: $S(10^k+b)=1+b\le0$, which is impossible since $10^k+b$ is a positive integer.

So $b=0$ and $P(x)=x$, which clearly works.

**Answer: $P(x)=c$ for an integer $1\le c\le9$, or $P(x)=x$.** ∎

prompt: Let $\tau(n)$ be the number of positive divisors of $n$. Let $\tau_1(n)$ be the number of positive divisors of $n$ which have remainders $1$ when divided by $3$. Find all possible integral values of the fraction $\dfrac{\tau(10n)}{\tau_1(10n)}$.
answer: All composite numbers, together with $2$ (equivalently: all even positive integers and all odd composite numbers).

solutions.title: A formula for $\tau_1$
solutions.body:
Write $p_i$ for primes $\equiv1\pmod3$ and $q_j$ for primes $\equiv2\pmod3$.

**Claim.** If $m=3^x\prod_ip_i^{a_i}\prod_{j=1}^tq_j^{b_j}$, then
$$\tau_1(m)=\prod_i(a_i+1)\cdot\Big\lceil\tfrac12\prod_j(b_j+1)\Big\rceil.$$
*Proof.* A divisor is $\equiv1\pmod3$ exactly when it contains no factor $3$ and the total exponent of the $q_j$'s is even; the exponents of the $p_i$ are free. Among the $N=\prod_j(b_j+1)$ choices of exponents $(e_1,\dots,e_t)$ with $0\le e_j\le b_j$, let $E$ have even sum and $O$ odd sum. Then
$$E-O=\prod_j\sum_{e=0}^{b_j}(-1)^e,$$
and each factor is $1$ if $b_j$ is even and $0$ if $b_j$ is odd. So $E=\frac N2$ if some $b_j$ is odd (then $N$ is even), and $E=\frac{N+1}2$ if all $b_j$ are even (then $N$ is odd). In both cases $E=\lceil N/2\rceil$. $\square$

**Computing the ratio.** Write $n=3^x2^y5^z\prod p_i^{a_i}\prod q_j^{b_j}$, where the $q_j$ are now the primes $\equiv2\pmod 3$ other than $2,5$ (note $2,5\equiv2\pmod3$). Then $10n=3^x2^{y+1}5^{z+1}\cdots$, so
$$\tau(10n)=(x+1)\prod(a_i+1)\cdot c,\qquad \tau_1(10n)=\prod(a_i+1)\cdot\lceil c/2\rceil,\qquad c=(y+2)(z+2)\prod_j(b_j+1).$$
- If $c$ is even, the ratio is $2(x+1)$.
- If $c$ is odd, the ratio is $\frac{2(x+1)c}{c+1}$. Since $\gcd(c,c+1)=1$, it is an integer only when $c+1\mid2(x+1)$, and then it equals $kc$ with $k=\frac{2(x+1)}{c+1}\ge1$. Here $c$ odd means $y$ and $z$ are odd, so $y+2\ge3$, $z+2\ge3$, and $c$ (hence $kc$) is composite.

So every integral value is an even number or an odd composite number.

**All of these occur.** For an even number $2m$, take $n=3^{m-1}$: then $c=2\cdot2$ is even and the ratio is $2m$. For an odd composite $N=uv$ with odd $u,v\ge3$, take $n=3^{(N-1)/2}\,2^{u-2}\,5^{v-2}$: then $c=uv=N$ and $2(x+1)=N+1=c+1$, so the ratio is $c=N$.

**Answer: the possible values are $2$ and all composite numbers** (i.e. all even positive integers and all odd composites). ∎

prompt:
Define $P(n)=n^2+n+1$. For any positive integers $a$ and $b$, the set
$$\{P(a),P(a+1),P(a+2),\dots,P(a+b)\}$$
is said to be *fragrant* if none of its elements is relatively prime to the product of the other elements. Determine the smallest size of a fragrant set.

Let $n$, $m$, $k$ and $l$ be positive integers with $n\ne1$ such that $n^k+mn^l+1$ divides $n^{k+l}-1$. Prove that

- $m=1$ and $l=2k$; or
- $l\mid k$ and $m=\dfrac{n^{k-l}-1}{n^l-1}$.
answer: Adding the divisor, $N=n^k+mn^l+1$ divides $n^{k+l}+n^k+mn^l$. Cancel the power of $n$ (coprime to $N$): $N$ divides $n^l+mn^{l-k}+1$ if $l\ge k$, or $n^k+n^{k-l}+m$ if $l<k$. In each case that number is less than $2N$, so it equals $N$.

solutions.title: Add the divisor and compare sizes
solutions.body:
Let $N=n^k+mn^l+1$. Then $N\mid n^{k+l}-1$ implies
$$N\mid(n^{k+l}-1)+N=n^{k+l}+n^k+mn^l,$$
and $\gcd(N,n)=1$.

**Case $l\ge k$.** Here $n^{k+l}+n^k+mn^l=n^k\big(n^l+1+mn^{l-k}\big)$, so $N\mid n^l+mn^{l-k}+1$. This number is positive and
$$n^l+mn^{l-k}+1\le n^l+mn^l+1\le2mn^l+1<2N,$$
so it equals $N$: $n^l+mn^{l-k}=n^k+mn^l$, i.e.
$$m\big(n^l-n^{l-k}\big)=n^l-n^k.$$
If $m\ge2$, then since $n^{l-k}\le\frac12n^l$, the left side is at least $2n^l-2n^{l-k}\ge n^l>n^l-n^k$, a contradiction. So $m=1$, and then $n^{l-k}=n^k$, i.e. $l=2k$.

**Case $l<k$.** Here $n^{k+l}+n^k+mn^l=n^l\big(n^k+n^{k-l}+m\big)$, so $N\mid n^k+n^{k-l}+m$. Since $n^{k-l}\le n^k$ and $m<2mn^l$,
$$n^k+n^{k-l}+m<2n^k+2mn^l+2=2N,$$
so $n^k+n^{k-l}+m=n^k+mn^l+1$, i.e. $m(n^l-1)=n^{k-l}-1$ and
$$m=\frac{n^{k-l}-1}{n^l-1}.$$
This is an integer, so $n^l-1\mid n^{k-l}-1$. Since $\gcd(n^u-1,n^v-1)=n^{\gcd(u,v)}-1$ and $n\ge2$, this gives $\gcd(l,k-l)=l$, i.e. $l\mid k-l$, hence $l\mid k$. ∎

prompt:
Let $a$ be a positive integer which is not a square number. Denote by $A$ the set of all positive integers $k$ such that
$$k=\frac{x^2-a}{x^2-y^2}\tag{1}$$
for some integers $x$ and $y$ with $x>\sqrt a$. Denote by $B$ the set of all positive integers $k$ such that (1) is satisfied for some integers $x$ and $y$ with $0\le x<\sqrt a$. Prove that $A=B$.
answer: Rewrite (1) as $ky^2-(k-1)x^2=a$. The Pell-type maps $(x,y)\mapsto\big((2k-1)x\pm2ky,\ (2k-1)y\pm2(k-1)x\big)$ preserve solutions; the "$+$" map increases $x$ (from $x<\sqrt a$ to beyond $\sqrt a$) and the "$-$" map (taking absolute values) decreases $x$ (from $x>\sqrt a$ to below $\sqrt a$).

solutions.title: A Pell-type descent and ascent
solutions.body:
For a positive integer $k$, equation (1) is equivalent to
$$ky^2-(k-1)x^2=a.\tag{2}$$
Indeed, (1) implies (2). Conversely, (2) excludes $x^2=y^2$ (that would give $y^2=a$, a square), so (2) implies (1). Also $k=1$ is impossible ($y^2=a$), so $k\ge2$. Signs of $x,y$ do not matter in (2).

**Claim.** If $(x,y)$ satisfies (2), so do
$$x'=(2k-1)x\pm2ky,\qquad y'=(2k-1)y\pm2(k-1)x .$$
*Proof.* Expanding $k{y'}^2-(k-1){x'}^2$, the cross terms are $\pm4k(k-1)(2k-1)xy\mp4k(k-1)(2k-1)xy=0$. The remaining coefficients are $k(2k-1)^2-(k-1)(2k)^2=k$ for $y^2$ and $4k(k-1)^2-(k-1)(2k-1)^2=-(k-1)$ for $x^2$. So $k{y'}^2-(k-1){x'}^2=ky^2-(k-1)x^2=a$. $\square$

**$B\subseteq A$.** Let $k\in B$, with a solution $0\le x<\sqrt a$ and (without loss of generality) $y\ge0$. In (1) the numerator $x^2-a$ is negative and $k>0$, so $y>x$, i.e. $y\ge x+1$. Take the "$+$" map: $x'=(2k-1)x+2ky\ge x+2k>x$ and $y'\ge0$. If still $x'<\sqrt a$, repeat; each step increases $x$ by at least $2k$. After finitely many steps we reach a solution with $x>\sqrt a$ (equality is impossible since $a$ is not a square). So $k\in A$.

**$A\subseteq B$.** Let $k\in A$, with a solution $x>\sqrt a$ and $y\ge0$. Now the numerator of (1) is positive, so $x>y\ge0$. Take the "$-$" map, replacing $x',y'$ by their absolute values: $x'=|(2k-1)x-2ky|$. We show $x'<x$, i.e. $-x<(2k-1)x-2ky<x$.
- The left inequality is $2kx>2ky$, which holds since $x>y$.
- The right inequality is $(k-1)x<ky$. From (2), $ky^2=a+(k-1)x^2>(k-1)x^2$, so $k^2y^2>k(k-1)x^2>(k-1)^2x^2$, i.e. $ky>(k-1)x$.

So we get a solution with $0\le x'<x$. If still $x'>\sqrt a$, repeat. The values of $x$ strictly decrease through nonnegative integers, so eventually $0\le x<\sqrt a$. Thus $k\in B$.

Hence $A=B$. ∎

prompt: Denote by $\mathbb N$ the set of all positive integers. Find all functions $f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ such that for all positive integers $m$ and $n$, the integer $f(m)+f(n)-mn$ is nonzero and divides $mf(m)+nf(n)$.
answer: $f(n)=n^2$ (first $f(1)=1$, then $f(p)=p^2$ for primes $p\ge7$, then use a large prime $p$ with an arbitrary $n$).

solutions.title: Primes first, then a large prime
solutions.body:
Write the condition as
$$f(m)+f(n)-mn\ \mid\ mf(m)+nf(n).\tag{1}$$

**$f(1)=1$.** With $m=n=1$: $2f(1)-1\mid2f(1)$, so $2f(1)-1\mid1$, and since $f(1)\ge1$ we get $f(1)=1$.

**$f(p)=p^2$ for primes $p\ge7$.** With $m=p$, $n=1$: $d=f(p)-p+1$ divides $pf(p)+1$, hence also
$$pf(p)+1-p\,d=p^2-p+1 .$$
If $d=p^2-p+1$, then $f(p)=p^2$. Otherwise, as $p^2-p+1$ is odd and positive, either $d<0$ or $d$ is a proper divisor, so $d\le\frac{p^2-p+1}3$ in all cases. Then
$$f(p)\le\frac{p^2+2p-2}{3}.\tag{2}$$
With $m=n=p$: $2f(p)-p^2\mid2pf(p)$, hence $2f(p)-p^2\mid2pf(p)-p(2f(p)-p^2)=p^3$. By (2) and $f(p)\ge1$,
$$-p^2<2f(p)-p^2\le\frac{2(p^2+2p-2)}3-p^2=-\frac{(p-2)^2}{3}<-p,$$
where the last step uses $p^2-7p+4>0$ for $p\ge7$. No divisor of $p^3$ (that is, $\pm1,\pm p,\pm p^2,\pm p^3$) lies strictly between $-p^2$ and $-p$. This contradiction shows $f(p)=p^2$.

**General $n$.** Fix $n$ and take a prime $p\ge7$ with $p>f(n)$ and $p>n$. With $m=p$ in (1),
$$p^2-pn+f(n)\ \mid\ pf(p)+nf(n)-n\big(f(p)+f(n)-pn\big)=p^3-np^2+pn^2=p(p^2-pn+n^2).$$
Since $p\nmid f(n)$, $p$ does not divide $p^2-pn+f(n)$, so this divisor is coprime to $p$ and
$$p^2-pn+f(n)\ \mid\ p^2-pn+n^2,\quad\text{hence}\quad p^2-pn+f(n)\ \mid\ n^2-f(n).$$
For large $p$ the divisor $p^2-pn+f(n)$ exceeds $|n^2-f(n)|$ in absolute value, so $n^2-f(n)=0$. Thus $f(n)=n^2$ for every $n$.

**Check.** For $f(n)=n^2$: $f(m)+f(n)-mn=m^2-mn+n^2>0$, and $mf(m)+nf(n)=m^3+n^3=(m+n)(m^2-mn+n^2)$ is divisible by it.

**Answer: $f(n)=n^2$.** ∎

prompt: Let $n$ be an odd positive integer. In the Cartesian plane, a cyclic polygon $P$ with area $S$ is chosen. All its vertices have integral coordinates, and the squares of its side lengths are all divisible by $n$. Prove that $2S$ is an integer divisible by $n$.
answer: Reduce to $n=p^t$ and induct on the number of vertices: triangles follow from Heron's formula $16S^2=n^2(\dots)$; otherwise some diagonal has square divisible by $p^t$ (if none did, Ptolemy would force $\nu_p(A_1A_m^2)$ to decrease strictly along $m$, a contradiction), so cut along it.

prompt: Find all polynomials $P(x)$ of odd degree $d$ and with integer coefficients satisfying the following property: for each positive integer $n$, there exist $n$ positive integers $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n$ such that $\frac12<\frac{P(x_i)}{P(x_j)}<2$ and $\frac{P(x_i)}{P(x_j)}$ is the $d$-th power of a rational number for every pair of indices $i$ and $j$ with $1\le i,j\le n$.
answer: $P(x)=a(rx+s)^d$ with integers $a\ne0$, $r\ge1$, $\gcd(r,s)=1$. (Depress the polynomial to $Q(y)$ with no $y^{d-1}$ term. Take a large prime $p\equiv2\pmod d$, and $d+1$ of the $y_i$ congruent mod $p$. Size estimates force $\frac{Q(y_i)}{Q(y_1)}=\big(\frac{y_i}{y_1}\big)^d$, so $Q(y)=b_dy^d$.)

solutions.title: Depressed polynomial, a large prime, and size estimates
solutions.body:
The $x_i$ are understood to be distinct (otherwise all $x_i$ equal would work for every $P$).

**These polynomials work.** If $P(x)=a(rx+s)^d$, take $x_i=N+i$ with $N$ large. Then $\frac{P(x_i)}{P(x_j)}=\Big(\frac{rx_i+s}{rx_j+s}\Big)^d$ is a $d$-th power of a rational, and it tends to $1$ as $N\to\infty$, so it lies in $(\frac12,2)$ for large $N$.

**Necessity.** Replacing $P$ by $-P$ changes nothing, so let $P(x)=a_dx^d+a_{d-1}x^{d-1}+\dots+a_0$ with $a_d>0$. Substitute $y=da_dx+a_{d-1}$ and define $Q(y)=P(x)$. Then
$$Q(y)=b_dy^d+b_{d-2}y^{d-2}+\dots+b_0$$
has rational coefficients, $b_d>0$, and no $y^{d-1}$ term. Let $B=\max|b_j|$, and let $c$ be a positive integer with $cQ\in\mathbb Z[y]$ (e.g. $c=(da_d)^d$). Distinct positive integers $x_i$ give distinct integers $y_i$, and since we may discard finitely many $x_i$ (by taking $n$ larger), we may assume all $y_i$ exceed any constant depending only on $P$. In particular:
$$|Q(y)|<2By^d,\qquad \tfrac12<\tfrac{Q(y_i)}{Q(y_j)}<2\ \Rightarrow\ \tfrac13<\tfrac{y_i^d}{y_j^d}<3.\tag{$*$}$$

Fix a prime $p\equiv2\pmod d$ (Dirichlet's theorem gives infinitely many, as $d$ is odd), with $p\nmid c$, and so large that
$$|b_d|\,p^{1/d}>21(d-1)B(2cB)^{1/d}.\tag{$**$}$$
Then $\gcd(p-1,d)=1$. Take $n>dp$; by pigeonhole, $d+1$ of the $y_i$, say $y_1,\dots,y_{d+1}$, are congruent mod $p$. Then $cQ(y_i)\equiv cQ(y_1)\pmod p$.

**Claim.** $\dfrac{Q(y_i)}{Q(y_1)}=\dfrac{y_i^d}{y_1^d}$ for $2\le i\le d+1$.

*Proof.* The ratio is positive and a $d$-th power, so write $\frac{Q(y_i)}{Q(y_1)}=\frac{l^d}{m^d}$ with coprime positive integers $l,m$. Then $\frac12<\frac{l^d}{m^d}<2$, and $m^d$ divides $cQ(y_1)$ divided by $\gcd\big(cQ(y_i),cQ(y_1)\big)$. Clearing denominators in $m^dQ(y_i)=l^dQ(y_1)$:
$$b_d\,(my_i-ly_1)\big(m^{d-1}y_i^{d-1}+m^{d-2}y_i^{d-2}ly_1+\dots+l^{d-1}y_1^{d-1}\big)=-\sum_{j=0}^{d-2}b_j\big(m^dy_i^j-l^dy_1^j\big).\tag{3}$$
Using $l^d<2m^d$ and $y_1^{d-2}<3y_i^{d-2}$, the right side has absolute value at most $(d-1)B\cdot7m^dy_i^{d-2}$. Suppose $my_i-ly_1\ne0$.

- *If $p\mid cQ(y_1)$:* then $p$ also divides $cQ(y_i)$, so $m^d\le\frac{|cQ(y_1)|}{p}<\frac{2cB}{p}y_1^d$ and $m<\big(\frac{2cB}p\big)^{1/d}y_1<3\big(\frac{2cB}p\big)^{1/d}y_i$. The left side of (3) has absolute value at least $|b_d|m^{d-1}y_i^{d-1}$, while the right side is at most $21(d-1)B\big(\frac{2cB}{p}\big)^{1/d}m^{d-1}y_i^{d-1}$. This contradicts $(**)$.
- *If $p\nmid cQ(y_1)$:* reducing $l^d\,cQ(y_1)=m^d\,cQ(y_i)$ mod $p$ gives $l^d\equiv m^d$. Here $p\nmid m$ (otherwise $p\mid l$ too). Since $\gcd(d,p-1)=1$, the map $t\mapsto t^d$ is injective on $(\mathbb Z/p)^\times$, so $l\equiv m\pmod p$. Then $my_i-ly_1\equiv m(y_i-y_1)\equiv0\pmod p$, so $|my_i-ly_1|\ge p$. Now $m^d\le|cQ(y_1)|$ gives $m<3(2cB)^{1/d}y_i$. The left side of (3) is at least $|b_d|\,p\,m^{d-1}y_i^{d-1}$ and the right side at most $21(d-1)B(2cB)^{1/d}m^{d-1}y_i^{d-1}$, again contradicting $(**)$.

Hence $my_i=ly_1$, and $\frac{Q(y_i)}{Q(y_1)}=\big(\frac lm\big)^d=\big(\frac{y_i}{y_1}\big)^d$. $\square$

**Conclusion.** The polynomial $Q(y_1)y^d-y_1^dQ(y)$ has degree at most $d$ and vanishes at the $d+1$ distinct values $y_1,\dots,y_{d+1}$, so it is identically zero. Hence $Q(y)=b_dy^d$, that is,
$$P(x)=a_d\Big(x+\frac{a_{d-1}}{da_d}\Big)^d.$$
Write $\frac{a_{d-1}}{da_d}=\frac sr$ in lowest terms with $r\ge1$. Then $P(x)=\frac{a_d}{r^d}(rx+s)^d$. Its constant term $\frac{a_ds^d}{r^d}$ is an integer and $\gcd(r,s)=1$, so $r^d\mid a_d$ (if $s=0$ then $r=1$). So $P(x)=a(rx+s)^d$ with the integer $a=a_d/r^d$ (allowing for the sign change at the start).

**Answer: $P(x)=a(rx+s)^d$ with integers $a\ne0$, $r\ge1$ and $\gcd(r,s)=1$.** ∎
